items.title: Most adult humans can't digest milk — and that's normal
items.claim: Babies make lactase to digest lactose in milk. In most of the world's adults, lactase production switches off after weaning. Adult milk-drinkers — common in Europeans and some African and Middle Eastern populations — carry a recently evolved mutation.

options.text: Adult lactose intolerance is ancestral; lactase persistence is a derived trait that arose in populations that domesticated dairy animals in the last 10,000 years

items.reveal:
Roughly 65 percent of adult humans globally show reduced lactase production after weaning. Lactase persistence is most common in northern Europeans (around 90 percent), some West African pastoralist groups, and some Middle Eastern populations.

Different regulatory mutations independently produced this trait in different lineages — convergent evolution. The European variant (a single nucleotide change near the LCT gene, called T-13910) is dated to about 5,000 to 10,000 years ago, coinciding with cattle domestication.

Dairy farming and lactase persistence appear to have co-evolved: ancient DNA shows farmers drank milk before persistence was common, suggesting cultural use (fermented dairy, lower lactose) preceded biological adaptation. As populations relied more on milk, the persistence allele was strongly selected.
items.why: European diets are taken as a baseline; lactose intolerance is treated as a disorder. Globally, lactose intolerance IS the baseline — milk drinking adults are the rare ones.

items.title: Your heart pumps 7000 litres of blood every day
items.claim: Resting heart rate ~70 bpm. Stroke volume ~70 ml. Cardiac output ~5 litres per minute, 7200 litres per day. Over an average lifetime: 250 million litres pumped — enough to fill 100 Olympic swimming pools.
items.prompt: How can such a small muscle pump so much?

options.text: The heart is hollow so volume doesn't matter

Continuous high turnover: each heartbeat moves a small volume, but ~100,000 beats per day add up; cardiac muscle is uniquely adapted (intercalated discs, dense mitochondria, near-zero anaerobic capacity) to never tire
Most of the volume is recycled within the heart
Blood is much lighter than water

items.reveal:
Cardiac muscle (myocardium) is structurally distinct from skeletal muscle. Cells are short, branching, with one or two nuclei, joined by intercalated discs containing gap junctions that synchronise contraction.

About 30% of cardiac muscle volume is mitochondria (vs 1-2% in skeletal muscle). The heart oxidises fatty acids preferentially and never fatigues under normal conditions.

It's also self-rhythmic: the sinoatrial node (in the right atrium) generates 70-80 spontaneous depolarisations per minute, propagated via the AV node and Purkinje fibres. Cut all nerves to the heart and it keeps beating (just at a different rate).

Under exercise, cardiac output can rise to 25+ L/min (5x resting) — by increasing both heart rate and stroke volume. Elite athletes have larger left ventricles and lower resting heart rates (40s, even 30s).

The heart's own coronary arteries feed it. Block one and the muscle downstream dies in minutes — myocardial infarction.
items.why: Continuous lifelong pumping sounds impossible. Heart muscle isn't ordinary muscle — it's a specialised contractile tissue evolved precisely never to stop.

items.title: Remove three quarters of a liver and it grows back
items.claim: Humans can lose 70-75% of their liver (in surgery or donation) and regrow it to original size within weeks. The liver is the only solid human organ with this level of regenerative ability. Even other strongly regenerative tissues (skin, bone marrow) can't grow back this much organ.

options.text: A reservoir of liver stem cells expands

Mature hepatocytes (normally quiescent) re-enter the cell cycle and divide; growth factors (HGF, EGF, IL-6) signal the remaining cells to proliferate until the original organ mass is restored, then stop
Surrounding organs grow into the missing space
The bile duct generates new liver tissue

items.reveal:
Normal adult liver: hepatocytes (~80% of liver cells) sit in G0, dividing at most once every year or two. Cellular workhorses doing biochemistry, not growing.

After partial hepatectomy (surgical removal): within hours, growth factors (hepatocyte growth factor HGF, EGF, TGF-alpha) surge in the portal blood. Hepatocytes enter S phase by 24-48 hours, divide, and continue dividing until liver mass returns. Then they switch off and resume their quiescent state.

Full regeneration in 2-3 weeks. Donors who give part of their liver for transplant recover their original liver mass and function.

Limit: the regeneration requires intact liver remnant. Cirrhotic livers — where hepatocytes have been replaced by scar tissue — cannot regenerate. Acute liver failure with widespread cell death may also overwhelm the regenerative response.

The Prometheus myth (vulture eats his liver, which regrows nightly) suggests ancient Greek anatomists may have noticed liver regeneration. Modern molecular understanding mostly dates from the 1980s-90s.

The liver's regenerative capacity is one of the foundations of living donor transplants — a partial donation to a recipient leaves both with functional livers.
items.why: Major organ regrowth seems out of reach for mammals. The liver does it routinely — and the molecular signals are now well enough understood to be co-opted for transplant medicine.
